Stage 2 of our journey · Synthetic test system: 450 wells

Better data, or a better model? Three approaches on the same wells

We gave three forecasting approaches the same 450 simulated wells and the same test: learn from 150 days, then forecast the next 30 against the hidden truth. The comparison separates the value of better readings from the value of a smarter model.

The headline

Switching from pump-start readings to resting-level readings cut the error from about 4.2 m to 0.5 m. Adding pumping, rain and supply information cut it to about 0.3 m. Better data mattered most.

How to use this page

Pick a well to compare the three approaches on it. Scroll down for the error tables, the side-by-side matrix, and the Stage 1 real-data panel.

Keep in mind

The test system is simulated and follows its own assumptions. Real-well accuracy has to be measured on real long-term records.

Decoder: what the labels on this page mean
M1: trend from pump-start readings
The Stage 1 method: follow each well's recent trend, using the level recorded when a pump starts.
M2: M1 plus rainfall
The same trend, adjusted for typical rainfall.
M3: the driver model
Uses resting-level readings plus pumping, rain, water supply and demand to predict each day's change.
M1 static
M1 fed resting-level readings instead, which shows what better data alone achieves.
Persistence / 60-day trend
Simple yardsticks: "nothing changes", and "extend the last 60 days' line".
Average error (MAE)
How far off the forecasts were, on average, in metres. Lower is better.
RMSE
Another error measure that punishes big misses more heavily.
Bias
A lean in one direction: + means forecasts were too deep on average, − too shallow.
80% coverage
How often the true level landed inside the shaded range. For an honest "80%" range it should be about 80%.

One well. Three approaches.

Train: 1 Jan–30 May 2026 (150 days). Test: 31 May–29 Jun (30 days). Every model receives the actual future drivers it uses: M1 none; M2 rain; M3 volume, rain, supply and demand. This is a conditional-input test.

02 / Errors

Separate data quality from model complexity.

25 wells deliberately acquire measurement bias. All models see biased readings, while scoring uses the physical truth. Omitting these wells changes the evaluation population; it does not solve drift.

Model / referenceMAERMSEBias80% coverageMean half-widthWell-days

M1/M2 and the static ablation use the specified broad heuristic ranges; their high coverage is not calibration. Baselines have no claimed interval. Bias is prediction minus truth: positive means too deep.

03 / Overall comparison

Each model answers a different data situation.

QuestionM1 · Trend methodM2 · Rainfall scenarioM3 · 450-well driver

What this proves

On this constructed system, static readings remove most of the dynamic-reading error. Drivers improve the remaining forecast and enable ordered pumping/rain scenarios. The same test exposes sensor drift.

What this does not prove

It does not establish Bengaluru accuracy, sustainable yield, aquifer recharge rates, or six-month to five-year reliability. Synthetic data favour their generating assumptions. Future drivers remain uncertain and drift requires calibration evidence.

Data-readiness path

M1 · Available now
Screened pump sessions and a clear dynamic-level definition.

M2 · Add public rainfall
Well locations and longer overlapping observations for real lag testing.

M3 · Company data contract
Standard static readings, calibration, pumped volume, supply/demand, nearby activity and ≥6–12 months of history.

The hidden-truth test page checks M3; it is not a fourth model. Full technical details are in the project's mathematical handoff document.

Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a year). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast.
